utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. You may already know, but nonetheless it's still my duty to remind you, that you are still bound by the declaration you have made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. Okay? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Defence will continue its examination, but may I ask you to make pauses between my questions and your answers for the benefit of the interpreters. Yesterday, we left off discussing a topic about -- in fact, we were discussing the Z-4 plan; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Z-4 plan, in January 1995, was it taken into consideration by the leadership of the Republic of Srpska Krajina? Did they discuss it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did consider the plan. I wasn't in the leadership. And the leadership laid conditions or, rather, they said that they would probably accept the plan if guarantees were issued that the UN forces should remain in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in connection with what you've just said, at that time, and we are talking about January 1995, were there any problems with the UNPROFOR mission in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Croatia requested that the UN forces leave the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will suffice. Now, after this position taken by the leadership of Republika Srpska Krajina, was UNPROFOR's mandate extended during 1995 at all?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember -- or, rather, do you know whether it was in March 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Can you tell us whether, after the mandate for UNPROFOR had been extended, whether the Z-4 plan, before Operation Flash, was offered to the Republic of Srpska Krajina again?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that it was offered to the leadership, and that there was a meeting held in Knin, an Assembly session, which was supposed to consider the Z-4 plan but that never came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the situation before the mandate was extended or after it was extended?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly when it was now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that on the 1st of May, or rather you confirmed that UNPROFOR's mandate was extended in March 1995, and you said that on the 1st of May, Croatia began its operation against the protected zone in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether anybody was held responsible because of that attack on Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether anybody was held accountable for the attack or the crimes perpetrated in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What knowledge do you have about this? For instance, do you know whether Mr. Martic committed any crimes during that operation in Western Slavonia, launched by the Croatian army and police?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't know Martic -- or, rather, I did know Milan Martic very well but he personally -- it was never recorded that he ever committed a crime. On the contrary, he was considered a brave man and people like that don't kill civilians and arrest civilians. That is something that the others do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Martic is being held responsible for killing civilians in Zagreb here. That is what he is accused of.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a research worker, scientist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I don't believe this arises out of the cross-examination. I don't think I asked him any questions about the shelling in Zagreb unless I've forgotten something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll withdraw that question, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague is quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in one of your answers you spoke about your impressions and said that Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Milosevic had been agreeing about the division of Bosnia; do you remember about that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you yourself present during the talks and negotiations between Mr. Milosevic and Tudjman on any occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I just learned about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. That's enough. Now, did you see a document ever which would confirm your impression that they had reached an agreement about Bosnia's division?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is something that Croatian authors write about, that there were negotiations and agreements about Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So was it on the basis of the writings of Croatian authors that you formed your impression that a compact of that kind had existed between Tudjman and Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my own personal opinion that I had formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you spoke about a statement made by Mr. Mesic to the Sabor, Croatian parliament, when, as president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, he returned to Zagreb from Belgrade. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have on the monitor, or rather on e-court, the video of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we take just a moment? This is a very brief clip. It's a very short statement which passes in just a fraction of a second.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I think I have done my duty. Yugoslavia doesn't exist anymore, and thank you very much."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that statement by Mr. Mesic? What did he say? Can you repeat the sentence we've just heard?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I think I have performed my task. Yugoslavia is no more," or it does not exist anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is that literally the exact words that Mr. Mesic just uttered?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I got the order wrong or, rather, I failed to provide the Trial Chamber with the exact text of that sentence which we have. I would like to ask the usher to hand it round to the Prosecution and to the Bench, and I apologise for not having done that straight away, and we can, if you wish, play the clip again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Mesic, as president of the Yugoslav state Presidency, is addressing people and says, "I think I have done my job or duty" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have not got the text in front of them in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: -- "and Yugoslavia exists no more." That's what we heard on the clip; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So the president of Yugoslavia who took the office says he has performed his task and that Yugoslavia exists no more. So that was his task: For Yugoslavia not to exist anymore?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would emerge --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Leading question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There have been several of them, actually. Mr. Milovancevic, the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I accept that, Your Honour. Let me rephrase that question. Do I have to wait for a ruling by the Chamber? I retracted that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, you don't have to wait for a ruling. You have retracted the question, Mr. Milovancevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I just want you to understand that rephrasing doesn't help because you have given the answer already. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We've dealt with that topic sufficiently. I'd just like to tender that clip into evidence as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what about the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, together with the translation. I apologise for omitting that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The video clip and the translation are accepted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 988.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this point in time, I have completed my redirect, in view of the Chamber's -- or, rather, may I ask additional questions that we put forward on the basis of the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You didn't see the filing, Mr. Milovancevic, the decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understood it in the way I asked the question. I wasn't jumping the gun in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to know whether you saw the decision. It was filed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, Witness, several questions linked to three areas, three topics, and the first is this: Your talks with Mr. Tudjman. Can you tell us when, Mr. Dakic, you met Mr. Tudjman at the beginning of 1990 and what the reason was?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had fairly regular meetings by -- with party representatives, parties in Croatia and we would usually in meet in Banski Dvori, and we could discuss current issues. And I remember on one occasion, Tudjman happened to be sitting opposite me, and since I knew him from before, I said, "Franjo, this isn't in order, the fact that the groundwork for your election campaign is the independent state of Croatia, the Ustasha movement, why you're using that as a basis." And he said in front of everybody, he said this, "Mile," he said, "afterwards, after the elections I will be quite a different man and won't mention that anymore." However, after the elections the same practice was continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that that was his answer to your remarks in front of others. Who were those others who attended those talks?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember all their names because things changed, of course, after that. But there were always about ten people there from different parties in Croatia. I omitted to state a moment ago that I said, "Well, don't do that. There will be blood up to our knees if that is put through. The Serbs will not be able to accept an Ustasha movement in any of its variations."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So those were representatives of other parties, were they?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, other parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand this question. When you say: "So those were representatives of other parties," who are these people you're talking about, Mr. Milovancevic? The people in whose presence he spoke? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: After the victory of the HDZ at the multi-party elections that were completed in May 1990, when the HDZ came into power, can you tell us what legal activities took place on the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mostly there were discussions about the constitution of Croatia, and in all the municipalities in Croatia, discussions and debates were held on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Thank you. The new Croatian government, within the frameworks of its duties and work, enact new laws and provisions for Croatia. Do you remember those that were enforced after the HDZ victory?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really remember them all just now, which rules and regulations. However, everything was geared towards the new constitution, and the new laws, regulations, provisions or whatever, were being drafted but with a view to waiting for the new constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, if I mentioned the law on holidays and non-working days in the Republic of Croatia, does that mean anything? Does it ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do know that this law on holidays was drafted, but you could feel the difference between the Catholics and the Orthodox over celebrating Christmas, other religious holidays and so on and so forth. The Christmas holidays for the Croats were two days long, I think. Now, when the Orthodox congregations had to celebrate their holidays and festivities they would have to ask in advance, and then people were afraid of doing so and didn't go to these festivities. And another saint day, Velika Gospa, was also celebrated and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And Christmas, that was a Catholic holiday, was it, and observed?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the Orthodox Christmas? Was that observed?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask the usher's help to distribute a document to the Bench and the Prosecution. It is the law on feast days and holidays or non-working days. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Do you have an additional copy for the interpreters, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It's just a brief text. We are not going to quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you do have a copy for them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And one more, please, for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have before you, Witness, the text of the law on holidays and non-working days that we mentioned. Is that the law that you referred to a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. That is the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender the text of the law as an exhibit, tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 989.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Milovancevic, will this translation be then completed or is it intended to be this kind of fragment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we translated just those provisions and articles which deal with feast days and holidays or holidays and non-working days because that is the law. It is the law on religious holidays, so we just translated those provisions, that particular article which we consider relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Which article?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And just to follow on what Judge Hoepfel asked you, what should we extract from this evidentially in relation to the relevant issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness spoke about those provisions within the law regulating state holidays, those dates which were considered state holidays. And from those dates, if you look at them, you can see the different dates, religious holidays and others, which were state holidays on the territory of the Republic of Croatia and the witness gave his comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So I should extract from it that these holidays were now more limited and that they were more in keeping with the Catholic faith than with the Orthodox?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's precisely what the witness was talking about. And it is in that sense that we provided this document and article of the law, because the law lists Catholic holidays; whereas for all other holidays, you need to request them, or they are not listed as holidays at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Are you now not testifying, Mr. Milovancevic, and giving us additional information?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I was answering the question from Her Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What I wanted to say, for completeness, I believe you should get the witness to relate the situation to the document, the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Which I was referring to before, with my question, which you could not yet answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Which article you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honours, I'd like to put specific questions to the witness on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you have the text of the law before you; do you see it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of one provision of this law which is to do with Christmas. Does the law provide for how many days you have holidays for Christmas?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It provides for two days of holidays for Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which article of the law regulates that specific issue?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Law on Christmas holidays, that's Article 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you stated that Serbs had one day to celebrate Christmas, which date did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was supposed to be on the 7th of January, but it wasn't proclaimed state holiday, a national holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that the Serbian Christmas, Orthodox Christmas, wasn't proclaimed a national holiday, what sort of an impact did it have on the Serb population? Were they able to celebrate Christmas?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were, on the proviso that the working people of Orthodox faith had to announce in advance that they would not come to the workplace on that date, and this evidently points to religious discrimination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, just before I forget, the witness now referred at page 12, line 24 to Article 4, obviously not translated in your translated exhibit. We'll have to get a translation of that, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, we will have the rest of the text translated and submitted to you at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the Feast of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary. Was it envisaged as a national holiday in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It normally falls on the 28th of August, and I mean that of the Orthodox faith, but it wasn't included in the text here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you now discussing the holiday celebrated by Catholics or members of the Orthodox faith?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Orthodox faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this law envisage the Feast of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary as a national holiday for the Catholics?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It is contained in the law, but the one for the members of the Orthodox faith is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which article of the law is that? I'm referring to the first page. Is that where that particular holiday is mentioned, Feast of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And it is mentioned here as falling on the 15th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to tender this document into evidence as a Defence Exhibit, and we take upon ourselves the obligation to submit the translation of the law at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. On the English translation as it now stands, can you please translate the words written after 15th of August? Because we don't understand them. And those words are exactly the same as they are on the B/C/S version. Can you give us the English version of what those words mean? You have been dealing with them now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to obtain my copy from the witness because I gave him my copy. Otherwise, we are going to encounter difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you look at the English version, you'll realise that the words after 15th of August are exactly the same as in B/C/S. They have not been translated. If you can translate them, particularly because you've dealt with them now in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have you finished with your leading, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I only wanted to confer with my colleagues. As for this date of the 15th of August, Velika Gospa, well, the term is simply untranslatable. It is the name of a holiday.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes it's the Feast of the Assumption of Our Virgin Mary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be precise, if you want me to, I can put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The 15th of August, Velika Gospa --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, you don't seem to understand what I'm trying to get. You have led this witness in evidence about this date and he has testified about it, and we have been told in evidence what -- by the interpreters what it relates to, okay? Now, I'm saying to you, as you undertook to translate the rest of this act, the rest of this law, into English, when you get to that point at the 15th of August, do remember to translate the English part, because the English part in this translation, against the 15th of August, you have not translated. That's all I'm saying. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. It is only now that I fully understand what you're saying. I was at a loss before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for the interruption. Your Honours, the procedure of translating the rest into English later, I have to say, is not particularly acceptable to the Prosecution because then I can't cross-examine. I assumed that only the English part, the part that had been translated, Article 1, was going to come into evidence, and I have no problem with that coming into evidence. But, you know, once there are references to Article 4, and I unfortunately can't read it but I can tell that it refers to other holidays and things, I would object to that coming into evidence, and I would propose that only Article 1, only what has been translated into English, be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Black, also Article 1 is not completed translated, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Black, then you should have -- aren't you late in the day? Shouldn't you have jumped at the first mention of Article 4? When I referred to Article 4 and asked that it be translated, there was a couple of lines after it had been referred to, I'm trying to find where it was first referred to. Unless you say Mr. Milovancevic must now provide you with a translation of Article 4 now, to enable you to cross-examine now, and then you can deal with the rest later?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm also trying to find the specific thing. At the time when it was tendered into evidence and became an exhibit at line -- excuse me, page 10, lines 21 to 25, we hadn't -- as far as I can tell, we had not gone into Article 4 and so I didn't object at that point. It was only later that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Then questions were raised by the Bench for clarification, and then there was a complaint from the Bench that the witness must explain, not him, and when he went to the witness to explain Article 4 came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. And I didn't feel like I could object to certainly not a question from Your Honours on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you could object to the fact that he's now referring to a part of the law that has not been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps that should have been the course, Your Honour. If that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now. My problem is it's now in evidence and what do we do at this stage? Is the solution really not that at least you be provided with a translation of at least Article 4 to enable you to cross-examine and then we can get the rest of the law later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Actually, I would like to have more than just the Article 4. It was my question. What article you're referring to. And then can the additional question by Judge Nosworthy, and you may then have forgotten to answer, but as the Article 1 is not complete, it's just a paragraph 1 in the translation, we will need to have a complete understanding of the law now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess you realise --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise but I have a proposal to make to the Bench in order to clarify the matter entirely. Since this law on holidays you have before you has only five articles, and the last article, Article 5, speaks of the date when the law should come into effect, whereas the Articles 2, 3 and 4 are quite short. In view of this, I'd like you to listen to the witness reading the full text out. We will hear the translation. But then we will have the official translation delivered to you later. So that there is no confusion and in view of the fact that only Article 1 was translated. We considered the Articles 2 to 5 only technical articles connected to Article 1, but in order for the matter not to stop there, we could proceed this way. And of course please accept my apologies because we could have had the entire law translated but because of the shortage of time we decided to have only one translated. So my proposal is to allow the witness to read out the remaining four articles of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I've got a problem with the way the Defence runs its defence. For instance, now this very Article 1 which the Defence knew in advance that they were going to deal with has not been completely translated. Why is the paragraph after the date 25th and 26th of December not translated into English? That at least should have been translated. There are words in B/C/S after the dates 25th, 26th and there is nothing in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you let the witness read Article 1 and the other articles -- because I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no. Don't side-step my question. My question is: Why didn't you translate these last words after 25, 26th of December? You knew you were going to use Article 1, and those words are part of Article 1. And they are just about two lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was an error in translation where one part was overlooked. This is the part of Article 1 which regulates how the holidays are to be used and we will have this translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't testify, please. Don't tell us what they are. Tell us why you didn't put them or you have told us you've overlooked the place. That's the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm merely trying to explain to you why we failed to do that. My proposal is for the witness to read out the four articles, and the English translation of all the four articles -- rather, of all the five articles will be submitted to the Bench. And please accept our apologies for the fact that we haven't done this right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Milovancevic. At quarter to you stop your examination-in-chief, remember. That's 30 minutes for three topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll bear this in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading the entire proclamation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please read Article 1 of the text.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Holidays in the Republic of Croatia are: 1st of January, new year. 1st of May, Labour Day. 30th of May, Statehood Day. 22nd of July, Day of the Anti-Fascist Struggle. 15th of August, Velika Gospa, Feast of the Assumption. 25 and 26 of December, Christmas holidays."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. Please now read the part of the text that wasn't translated.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Citizens of the Republic of Croatia shall not work on the dates under paragraph 1 of the present article and will be entitled to remuneration for those dates. If one of the dates from Article 1 -- from paragraph 1 of this Article is a Sunday, the holiday will fall on the next working day."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please now read Article 2 of the law.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The non-working days in the Republic of Croatia, in respect of which workers will be entitled to a remuneration, shall be the 6th of January, 7th of January, Easter Monday, the second day of Easter, Bajram, Bajram, and the 1st of November, All Saints' Day. Members of the Jewish community shall be entitled to be absent from work on Yom Kippur and Rosh Hashanah and shall be entitled to remuneration for those dates. Muslims shall be entitled to be absent from work on greater Bajram and shall be entitled to remuneration." Article 3: "The government of the Republic of Croatia may decide which state agencies and other public agencies, as well as legal and natural persons, shall be duty-bound to work on holidays and on working days in the Republic of Croatia." Article 4: "With the date of enforcement of this law, the following piece of legislation shall become null and void: The law on the proclamation of the 27th of July a national holiday, Official Gazette number 111/47. The law on celebrating the All Saints' Day, or the day of remembrance of the dead, Official Gazette number 46/89. The law on Christmas holidays, Official Gazette number 53/90, Article 46, paragraph 1 of the labour law, Official Gazette number 19/90. The words 'from paragraph 1 of this article' in paragraph 2 of the same article shall be deleted. With the date of enforcement of this law, the law on holidays of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, Official Gazette of the SFRY number 6/73, shall become null and void in the territory of the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please wait? I haven't -- the interpreter hasn't finished translating.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 5: "This law shall come into force with the date of its publication in the Official Gazette, number 960-01/91-01/02, Zagreb, 21st of March, 1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Have you read out the entire text? Do you think it is complete?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the complete text of the law. It will be submitted to you as a full English translation. We have only given to you so far the fraction of Article 1. In light of this, I don't know if the Defence should at this point -- or, rather, I'm advised by my colleague that this has already become part of evidence. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the law on Croatian arts and sciences?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I asked you if you read the decision yesterday. The decision gave you ten minutes per topic and you started this evidence-in-chief at quarter past. That's been 30 minutes already and more. It's actually now 35 minutes. You are supposed to have finished your examination-in-chief on the topics you wanted to lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have only one or two questions and I will soon complete my examination. We have spent a lot of time on these technical difficulties and I kindly appeal to the Bench to take this into consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Put the two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As president of the Commission for War Crimes in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, you collected information on such incidents involving Serb citizens and the suffering, as you indicated it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the suffering of the Serb people in the territory of Slavonia, specifically Sisak, in the period of 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of the exodus which took place in late 1991, where the Serb population had to leave the area, was forced to leave the area, and this constituted a large-scale ethnic cleansing in the territory of Croatia, specifically Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The villages of Kinjacka, Cakale, Trnjani, and the Croatian police in Sisak. Do these ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have information even with me here, a manuscript in my case here with me, that is the information about the Croatian forces committing genocide on the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to distribute a document to the Bench, the Prosecution and the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, your time is up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I think you asked an additional question before that, and there was no answer as we then had the discussion about the time you already had used. So can the witness please answer the question on the law on Croatian arts and sciences, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the law governing the Academy of Arts and Sciences of Croatia. The academy was not established under this name but it was established in 1866 in Zagreb and it was called the Yugoslav Academy of Arts and Sciences at the time. In 1941, the independent state of Croatia changed its name into the Croatian Academy of Arts and Sciences. After World War II, it was again named the Yugoslav Academy of Arts and Sciences. It is a well-known scholarly academy in Croatia, and up until 1990, it was called the Yugoslav Academy of Arts and Sciences. At that point in time, Croatia again renamed it Croatian Academy of Arts and Sciences. But interestingly enough, the law adopted at the time reads that the Croatian Academy of Arts and Sciences shall -- or, rather, dates back to the Croatian Academy of Arts and Sciences established under that name for the first time during the fascist independent state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Bench does not have any more questions, I wish to say that I've completed my examination-in-chief, given the time constraints, and I just wish to note that the document that I asked be handed down will, in this case, be tendered differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand what is meant by "tendered differently."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the document we asked that be handed down was -- is actually moot now because in the meantime it became apparent that we don't have any more time. Therefore, we will seek to have that document admitted into evidence through a different witness. And I would like the document to be returned to the Defence team so that we spare ourselves additional photocopying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I hope I have very few questions on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dakic, it's my turn now to ask you a couple of more questions for a few minutes. And let me start on the law on holidays which you had read out to us. It's Exhibit 989. And I don't even think you need to look at it again. You've talked about now on re-examination about the differences or the lack of differences, in your view, between the independent state of Croatia in World War II and then the Croatian government in the 1990s. I think you've suggested that it was -- the government of the 1990s was an Ustasha government or had an Ustasha basis. Can you explain to me, sir, why one of the seven national holidays in Article 1 of this law, 22nd of July, was the day of the anti-fascist struggle?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that the 27th of July was celebrated in Croatia and Bosnia as uprising day, and then because Croatia wanted to be different from the others and to in a way undermine the struggle of the Serbian people during World War II, quite simply it had the 22nd of June [as interpreted] prevail when a group of communists, led by Janic Capa, fled from Sisak and took refuge in a forest and that was taken as the date of the day of the uprising, and that was a symbol of the separation between the two nations, which means that they only took this particular day and we reacted to that in no uncertain terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But, sir, this is a holiday celebrating the struggle against fascism, right? That's what the purpose of this holiday that we see in the law. That's what its purpose was.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was nothing compared to what happened in Croatia on the 27th of July as a massive uprising. All they did here was to take Croatian communists who fled from the town of Sisak to Brezovica and took to the woods there. There was no logic that that should be a state holiday, the fleeing of Serbs from Sisak and that they should have taken refuge in a forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think I'll move on to the next point. Thank you. You referred just at the end of your testimony to a law on the Croatian Academy of Arts and Sciences, and you pointed out how the actual law made reference to the Croatian Academy of Arts and Sciences from the World War II period. But isn't it correct that the law actually refers not just to that but it says it's where -- well, let me read it out to you and tell me if this accords with your memory. It says: "The academy continues the work and is the legal successor of the Yugoslav Academy of Arts and Sciences established in 1866 as the highest scientific body of all southern Slavs. Croatian Academy of Arts and Sciences from 1941 to 1945, and from 1947 to 1991, again the Yugoslav Academy of Arts and Sciences." And that's correct, right? It referred to all those prior bodies, it made itself the successor of all those prior bodies?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to react to that, you know, because any mention of --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, before you tell me about the reaction, that's correct, that that's what the law said, right? It referred to all those bodies and not just to the Croatian Academy of Arts and Sciences from World War II; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct that mention is made of both, but what we found objectionable was that this mention was made of it during a period when crimes were committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That completes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This brings us to the end of your testimony, sir -- I beg your pardon. So sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I have no questions. Thank you, Judge. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a very few questions for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have told us right through your testimony and in particular yesterday that you are a historian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have you written books on history?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wrote and published ten books so far, and my latest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are these history books?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly history books, yes, but also -- I also write novels, short stories, poems and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's stick with the history books. What about -- the history of what countries or any countries did you write about? Or which people.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have written about my own people mostly, the nation to which I belong, but I also write about other nations in my books, especially the communality of the Serbian and Croatian people in Croatia, especially during the national liberation war, when this brotherhood and unity or communality came to the fore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then we will try and hone in on that. This communality of the Serbian people and the Croatian people in Croatia, what period does it span?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wrote a book entitled "Krajina Through the Centuries" which I have here with me, and in that book I wrote about the relationships and cooperation between the Croats and Serbs from the Vojna Krajina establishment in the 30s of the 16th century up to the present day. Krajina existed as a separate organisation under the direct rule of the Austro-Hungarian empire, the Austro-Hungarian monarchy, up until 1881, when the Vojina Krajina was abolished. And after that, Krajina, within the composition of Austria or, rather, the Austrian monarchy again but under the Hungarian crown, came into being again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have you written about the history of Croatia from 1990 to 1995 or covering that period?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I published a book in Knin on 1990 -- in 1990. That was the only book available during the war. It is called "Srpska Krajina," Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm talking about a book that would have been written after 1995, at least covering 1990 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has been translated into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I'm asking you if you have written a book that was after 1995, covering that period. Whether it has been translated is another matter. Have you?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote the book under the title of "Krajina Through the Centuries."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just listen to my question so that we can be quick. Have you written an account of Croatia which covers the period 1990 to 1995 at all? Have you? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have. And in that book, in that writing, did you deal with the relationships between the Croats in Croatia and the Serbs in Croatia in detail?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I gave a completely detailed description, since Vojna Krajina came into being, right up to the fall of Republika Srpska Krajina at the end of the war. And chronologically as well; I attached a chronology of the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you gave a very -- did you remember the incidents as you recorded them detailing the relationship between the Croats and the Serbs during that period 1990 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do you feel that you did -- you wrote a fair historical account, without being biased at all, in favour of one of the nations against the other?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I give a fair and unbiased account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why is it, then, that when you were being asked questions under cross-examination -- let me take it a step back, when you were being asked questions under examination -- in your statement, you have remembered a great deal of atrocities perpetrated by Croats against Serbs, and suddenly when you were asked about atrocities by Serbs against Croats, your memory suddenly became hazy and foggy, you couldn't remember dates, you couldn't remember incidents, you don't know anything about the incidents? Why is it so?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that on the Croatian side there are also historians writing mostly about the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just hold it, just hold it. I'm not asking you about other people. I'm asking you about you. I'm asking you if you wrote a fair account, a historical account, and you said yes. Now I'm asking you why do you show a tendency -- you were asked a question in cross-examination about why is it that you remember Croat attacks on Serbs and that Serb attacks on Croats you don't remember? You were asked specifically that question. And you just never gave an answer. You were evasive. You said that you were not in the front line so you did not have this information. But you were not also on the front line but you had information about attacks on Serbs. "I did not have access to documents about Serb crimes against Croats." That's one of the remarks you made in your evidence. Why was it so? It seems to me like you have a selective memory. Am I right in saying so?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think you're right on that score, because I wrote about and collected information about all victims. But, Your Honours, you cannot compare victims. We were the victims of the last war. We were ethnically cleansed. We were destroyed as a people, wiped out. In our houses over there, there is nobody left. It's a wasteland and a great injustice was done to my people, to my nation. Yes, the Croats fared badly during the war as well. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to stop you. I know all that. You've told us that in great detail. My problem with my question is that you have made out yourself in this court to be a historian, you know, so I expect you to treat the subject differently from the ordinary man who sees it from a biased perspective, who sees it from the perspective of the victim. I expect to you see it from the perspective of a historian, victim as you may very well be. I'm asking you a very simple question. And I'm not asking you about what you wrote. I'm asking you about what you did in this Court. You seemed to demonstrate a selective memory. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not selective memory, but I would say that it is a contribution to historiography to write the truth about anyone. And in this case I devoted my efforts to writing about my own people that suffered so terribly. That does not mean that I underestimate or condemn or do not blame people for the crimes committed against the Croats because with crimes you don't just kill one individual. I'm somebody who writes about crimes, but principally about crimes committed against my own nation. I don't condemn people writing about the victims amongst the Croatian people and I hold them in high esteem when they do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question. We now are here in a court of law and we are trying to find the truth, and you are testifying and telling us about crimes against your own people only and you have forgotten or don't remember the crimes against other people. How do you -- how would you suggest a court of law treats your account of events, given the way you remember events? If you were to give this Court advice on how to treat your evidence, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth about my writings and myself will become apparent when I publish my war diary. In my war diary, Your Honours, I write about all victims. Wherever I learnt that anybody was killed somewhere, I denounced that killing in all places and everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... will not be available to this Bench. What was important for this Bench was your testimony in this Court, and that is still the important part. Okay. You don't have any answer. Or do you?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am doing everything in my power to tell the truth, and please believe me when I say that I did tell the truth during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question to you was: Do you have any advice you would give to this Court on how to treat your evidence, given that you remembered certain parts and not others?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The advice is that there are other sources as well. I provided in my own way a description of it. There are other sources, of course, Your Honour. Let it not remain the matter rest with my testimony. Take into account that of others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For interest's sake, why did the papers call you Captain Darda? You said the mountain Darda is the highest mountain in Petrova Gora. Were you tall? Are you tall in physical stature or is it tallness in societal stature?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that area, I lived in Petrova Gora, I was the director of Petrova Gora, the Petrova Gora memorial, for 28 whole years, and I did represent a sizeable entity. I was the most educated, perhaps, man in the area. I was a writer and I saw whole lot of crimes committed in Petrova Gora during World War II, and that is what led me to become a historian in the first place. So yes, I was somebody of some stature in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions. Any questions arising, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have some questions but I think it's time for the break now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm very sorry. I was completely oblivious of time. We will take the break and come back at quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I will have several questions for you. You do remember His Honour, Mr. Moloto, asking you whether you gave an accurate account of the events dating back to 1990 to -- from 1990 to 1995 in Croatia in the books you wrote. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't say in the books he wrote. I said in court here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for telling me that, but I was referring to one of the earlier questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And there were several questions which had to do with your books containing a chronology of these events; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether what you wrote in those books was truthful?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in the preface to my books I said that I strived to be quite truthful and consistent in writing about the events from that period, and that the truth came first. I'm really sorry that the Trial Chamber was -- did not have occasion to read my books.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were the -- were parts of your books read out in this courtroom during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember His Honour's question as to why you failed to remember the crimes against Croats in view of what you said, that you gave a fair and unbiased account?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can it be said, is it fair to say, that you do not recall any crimes committed against Croats?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It isn't fair to say that. Particularly in the area where I lived, in the area of Banija and Kordun, I was aware of the crimes. However, the scale at which these crimes were committed cannot -- one cannot even begin to compare them with the crimes that were committed against Serbs in that period and in World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the crimes are disproportionate and incomparable, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, specifically, this means that in the area of Krajina, about 7.000 people were killed in the area of Croatia. In the earlier war, there were about 12.000 to 15.000 Croats living there. And if you look at the makeup of the population, there is the -- the ratio is disproportionate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you talking about the disproportionate ratio of victims?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, disproportionate in -- and I was referring to the ratio of population versus victims. According to the statistics of the time, Serbs constituted 12 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the number of 7.000 people who were killed in Krajina and you mentioned 12 to 15.000 Croats. When you were giving these figures, did you mean to refer to those killed?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those killed and those who went missing and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that 7.000 people perished in the area of Krajina, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd say that 98 per cent of them were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall His Honour, Mr. Moloto, asking you about the fact that you didn't remember that the Serbs attacked Croats and that you were prevaricating, that you were being evasive in giving your answer to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't being evasive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did my learned friend, Prosecutor, allow to you explain why you wrote the books the way you wrote them?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no time for me to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall His Honour, Mr. Moloto, putting to you that you were expected to view matters from a point of view which is not lopsided and he also asked you about having selective memory; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was your point of view distorted in writing these accounts and did you in fact have selective memory?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot at any point be accused of having a selective memory. I was very much aware of crimes on either side, and I have a saying that -- that you don't just kill one person when you kill someone. That's what I always say to people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall mentioning that there was ethnic cleansing in Slavonia? Who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was referring to the Serbs being ethnically cleansed from Croatia. I mentioned yesterday the Serb intelligentsia that was being forced out of towns. My native area is a wasteland now. Nobody lives there, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who caused these victims?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the Croatian people, but the Croatian policies executed by the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the answer you've just given, what is your position and your knowledge as to the following: The Croatian victims who were killed at the hands of Serbs and their policies, were there such victims as well?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that our units never attacked anyone. They were always defensive, all the way from the log revolution up to the end of the war, whereas the other side was offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Going back to the questions put by Their Honours -- His Honour as to the fact that you were a historian, you completed schooling, faculty of philosophy, and you had your masters degree from the faculty of law. Based on this educational background, what prompted you to become a historian?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because, as a 11-year-old child I witnessed a terrible crime at Petrova Gora, where Ustasha forces killed 194 women, children and elderly, and I remember this child who came up to the dead bodies of her parents, saying, "Get up, get up, we have to leave." I recall that it was pinching cold outside, and I could see the steam rising from the ground, and I thought at the time that those were their souls going up to heaven. That was when I realised I have a vocation for history.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Going back to the questions concerning your nom de guerre, Captain Darda, and in this context the mount of Darda was mentioned, and you were asked whether you were high in physical or psychological stature. Do you recall that question?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do the physical traits bear any relevance in assessing a person's character, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I beg your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can I ask an additional question? Maybe starting from your memory of this experience when you saw this humidity going up from the ground and you were thinking of souls going to the heaven. What is the All Saints or All Souls' Day in your country?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Catholics celebrate the All Saints' Day on the 1st of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. But then do you also know something about All Souls' Day, 2nd of November? Is that a holiday or any special day, when people would go to cemeteries and visit graves of their families?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the Orthodox Church, there are several days around the year when one goes to the cemetery. That's the All Souls' Day. And for the Catholics, that's the 1st of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So may I ask some additional question concerning this law we were looking at, where it didn't have a complete translation but at least part of it, and so my first question would be what is the difference in the legal sense, do you know that, can you answer that question, between holidays and non-working days?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a national holiday proclaimed as such by the state. That's as far as the holidays are concerned. However, all the other faiths, their festivities, like those of the Orthodox and the Jewish communities, were given only non-working days, not holidays, and I believe this to have been a grave error to make in that piece of legislation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So you mean a difference between a public holiday where everything would be closed and a non-working day where members of this religious group are not obliged to work; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nobody works on holidays, on national holidays; whereas a non-working day is quite something else. A Sunday is also a non-working day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. So how was that before 1990 -- 1991? How was that during the times of the Socialist Republic of Croatia? Can we go through the text of this law again? Can you compare -- do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. I can -- maybe the usher can give that to you. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. So what was being celebrated, either as a holiday or as a non-working day, of these days, before?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of these days here, the 1st of January, the New Year's Day was celebrated. The 1st of May was celebrated, as Labour Day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then as for Christmas, well, I don't remember, but at least in the Orthodox community, I know that the communist authorities banned any celebrations of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Pardon? The communist authorities banned any celebrations of what?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a ban as such. It was a tacit ban. It was merely frowned upon, persons who went to church and celebrated church festivities and holidays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. And then we discussed about the differences between Catholic and Orthodox, but still Christian holidays, but maybe was there anything like protecting Jewish holidays and Muslim holidays in the Socialist Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one cannot see this clearly from this law, although it seems that they were all lumped together into this second category, second class.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What do you mean by "second class"?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply this: None of the Muslim or Jewish holidays or Orthodox holidays for that matter, were proclaimed national holidays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. But taking them being mentioned in this law, is that something new or was that already a tradition in the old days?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the way which the earlier legislation regulated these matters, but I do know that people who went to church were frowned upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not talking of going to a church but going to a temple or to a mosque now, yes? Let me get back to paragraph 1 of this Article 2. As you read it, it was translated but I don't really exactly remember. So you said it's a non-working day or holiday in January. Which one? Which days of January, please?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the month of January, 6 and 7 January; that's the Christmas Eve and Christmas Day in the Orthodox faith. Therefore, it's been stipulated as a non-working day and can be used by people as such but it was not stipulated as a national holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. So that would mean, practically speaking, that Orthodox Christians would have two Christmas, sort of, free days, on the 25th and 26th of December, and additionally their own Orthodox Christmas, the 6th and 7th of January; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had two days just as Catholics did. They had this entitlement to use it as a non-working day, but it was not stipulated as a national holiday. That is what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You know, I know that very well from my own experience. I'm a Protestant in a majority-Catholic country so I had always my own holidays in addition which was fine in school days, in the old school days. You understand maybe. Now, I think we understood that. There are no further questions on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: As to the 6th and 7th of January, Judge Nosworthy would like to ask some additional question for understanding. Yes? Please. I'm done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Is your substantive complaint, then, that the 6th and 7th of January for Serbs were not proclaimed as holidays as opposed to non-working days? Because under Article 2, the 6th and 7th of January are mentioned, are they not, as days on which you would not work?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gist of it is as follows: Why weren't both Christmases stipulated as the national holiday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if you will, please, deal with the situation as it is in the article. As it is in that article, the 6th and 7th of January would have been non-working days?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Non-working days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So on that day, would you have to work, or would it be a day off work?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But as far as I remember, in the implementation of the law, the position was as follows: Whoever wanted to have 6th -- the 6th or 7th January as a non-working day had to make previous notice to his employer that on the said dates he would not come to work. People avoided doing this, given the war circumstances and the difficult wartimes, and ended up not using those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: But would not the effect of it have been that you in fact got extra days than what Croatians got or Croats got? Or Catholics got? Because you got their day as a holiday and then you got your own religious days, in fact, as a working -- non-working day? So would your position not have been arguably more advantageous?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to persons shirking and idle would probably mean that this is advantageous. However, you see the point of the matter lies in the difference between a non-working day and a state holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So you would have wanted it to be a state holiday and to give Croats as well and Muslims that day also? Sorry, sorry, I have to make it religiously based, but it was also tied to the ethnic group as well. You would have preferred to have given Catholics and other religious groups a holiday on your religious holiday also then?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And you resented the fact -- the Orthodox faith members resented the fact that they actually had to submit an application to be absent from work on those days?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is what they resented the most, the fact that they had to announce their absence on these dates to the employer. The people were afraid of doing this, and this -- that is why the law created problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: As you may have noticed, I'm not Jewish, either in appearance and I'm not in faith. So could you please educate me, what days would Yom Kippur be? Are they referred to in Article 2?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states here that Yom Kippur is a day of conciliation or reconciliation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the calendar date. What month, what day?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess in fairness to the Defence, Mr. Milovancevic, you will have to ask questions arising from Judge Nosworthy's and Judge Hoepfel's questions before we let you ask your questions, Mr. Black. Mr. Milovancevic, any questions arising strictly from the questions by Judge Nosworthy and Judge Hoepfel?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Questions, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No questions, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Dakic, this brings us to the end of your testimony. The Chamber would like to thank you very much for coming to testify in these proceedings, and it appreciates that you take time off from your very busy schedule to come and be here. You may stand down. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I must say that I have felt the proceedings to be quite fair and correct, as was all the assistance related thereto. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to call the next witness and have him brought into the courtroom. His name is Zoran Lakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Lakic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As you know, I am Defence counsel for Milan Martic, and I'm going to be asking you questions in the first stage which is known as the examination-in-chief. Since you and I speak the same languages, please -- same language, please make pauses between my questions and your answers to give the interpreters a chance to do their job properly. I will try and keep my questions short and I'd like your answers to follow suit. As I said, try and speak as slowly as possible, to facilitate the work of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just remember, Mr. Milovancevic, that you have estimated him at five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us your full name and surname and where you were born?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Lakic. I was born in Benkovac, Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us your date of birth and what is your ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 12th of October, 1956, and I am a Serb by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you once again to do your best to speak slowly. You can see how your words come up on the transcript on the screens, so when the screen stops, that means they've finished. What education have you had, Mr. Lakic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
