utterances.text: I went to university. I'm a university graduate. I am professor of electrical engineering and I'm a graduate of electrical engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where do you live today and work today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: I live in Pozarevac, the Republic of Serbia, and I work as a professor of electrical engineering in the Nikola Tesla technical school in a place called Kostolac near Pozarevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Have you done your military service and, if so, where and when?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did complete my military service in Belgrade, in the school for reserve officers, in 1982-1983. Half my military service was spent in Belgrade, the reserve officers' school. And the rest in Samobor near Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Having completed your military service, where did you find employment first, and I'll link my next question up to this. That is to say my next question is: Did you find employment in the Territorial Defence perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. I continued working and doing what I had been doing before, working in the secondary school in Benkovac as a teacher. That's how I went to do my military service, as a teacher. Then one year after I had completed my military service, I worked for a brief period of time as a teacher again, and in 1985, in October, I found employment as an operations man or Chief of Staff in wartime of the Territorial Defence of Benkovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When in 1985 you worked in the Territorial Defence of Benkovac as chief of operations -- as an operative, could you tell us who was the commander of the Territorial Defence Staff, what his name was, and who the secretary was of the national defence, and which ethnic groups were there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: As far as the population of Benkovac is concerned, it is a multi-ethnic community. There were slightly more Serbs than Croats. And this national composition was reflected in the national cadres policy in the municipality and in military and police structures as well. I was the assistant commander and the commander himself was Dinko Drazina. He was a Croat. And in addition to me, there was another assistant for organisational and mobilisational affairs. His name was Magjan Pinter [phoen]; he was also a Croat. The assistant for the rear was Ljubo Kresovic. He was a Serb. And then the warehouse keeper was Mirko Slavojevic but he retired very quickly. But he was a Serb. And there was a clerk for general affairs, working in the administrative department or whatever it was called, and his name was Zeljko Lavanja; he was a Serb as well. The Secretariat for National Defence had a number of employees of mixed ethnic group. The secretary was a Serb, Gojko Tampolja, and the other employees, if you want me to give their names, I can do my best to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will suffice.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, this composition of the Territorial Defence Staff of Benkovac you said existed at the time when you gained employment there, when you became a member of the Territorial Defence in 1985. And tell us, how long did that structure last? What happened after that date?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: That structure existed from 1985, when I got a job there, until the Territorial Defence ceased to exist, which means that the Territorial Defence was established pursuant to documents dovetailed with republican laws governing national defence and Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia, and that law was fully in conformity with the national defence law of the SFRY; that is to say, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There was the peacetime formation for those structures and there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. The witness is very fast. The interpreter is struggling very hard to keep pace with you, sir. Can you please try to keep -- slow down? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I'll do my best to slow down. As I was saying, the Territorial Defence, pursuant to the law on national defence, was a peacetime formation up until 1991. And according to the wartime plans that existed, it exists -- there was the wartime formation, and the numbers were made up of the reserve force of military recruits and conscripts from Benkovac municipality. When they could not be deployed in the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Benkovac -- or, rather, nobody could be deployed there who was not recorded in the files of the Territorial Defence of Benkovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Have I understood you correctly? Did I understand you to say that it was only the inhabitants, to use simple language, that the inhabitants and citizens of Benkovac could have been members of the Territorial Defence within the Territorial Defence Staff for Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That was pursuant to the law and we adhered to that provision of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any changes occur within the Territorial Defence of Benkovac after the first multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, the commander of the Territorial Defence in peacetime and in war was Drazina, and in 1990, around the time of the elections, he left the Territorial Defence Staff, and went into private business.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Dinko Drazina what was a Croat, did you not, and he was the commander of the Territorial Defence, he occupied that post, am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Upon his departure, at the time of those first multi-party elections, who replaced him as commander?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: According to all the provisions that were in force at the time, legal provisions and military documents and wartime plans and everything regulating the life and work of the Territorial Defence, it was the Chief of Staff, which I was, during wartime automatically changed -- replaced the Territorial Defence commander but this -- and this post, at one of the subsequent Assembly meetings should appoint a new commander, and the selection is made once again according to the prevailing rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the command of the Territorial Defence of the municipality was appointed by the Assembly. Can you tell us which Assembly, when it comes to Benkovac, when we are talking about Benkovac? Were there any other conditions for the nomination, appointment of Territorial Defence commanders for the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff, whom I was, and the commander of the Territorial Defence, those posts and those individuals were elected by the Municipal Assembly, appointed. But with agreement from the Territorial Defence commander of the Republic of Croatia, which meant that I could not have been deployed, I could not occupy one of those positions or appointed to one of those positions, until the commander of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia agreed to my appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down. Slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The commander of the territory of the Republic of Croatia, Territorial Defence, at the time, was General Martin Spegelj, and he gave his approval for my appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were performing the function the commander of the Territorial Defence of Benkovac, who was your superior command, the first next superior command, up the chain of command compared to the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia according to the provisions in force at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: All the municipal staffs, Dalmatia, they were under the command of the zone command for Dalmatia, the headquarters of which were in Split. The commander of the Territorial Defence of Dalmatia at that point in time was Ante Marinov [phoen]. He was a colonel, an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army. The complete composition of that staff in Split was composed of members and officers of the Yugoslav People's Army at that time. A smaller number of workers were reserve officers, mostly from Split, so that was the structure of the national defence according to the national defence law of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the prevailing provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long were you in the position of commander of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I performed the function of Territorial Defence commander until the Territorial Defence was abolished which means up until the end of November 1992. Yes, 1992. I think it was the 27th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you a few questions now linked to the municipality of Benkovac itself. You have already told us that it was a multi-ethnic community and that the ratio of Serb inhabitants and Croat inhabitants was more or less the same, an equal number. What about the town of Benkovac? How many inhabitants did that have and what was the ethnic composition of its inhabitants in 1990?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, in 1990, the municipality of Benkovac was a multi-ethnic community. The overall municipality, in addition to the central town, Benkovac, was also made up of 64 villages distributed over a territory of some 620 square kilometres. The largest number of villages -- or most of the villages, ethnically speaking, were Serb villages. A lesser number were purely Croatian villages. For example, some 20 or 15 villages were of mixed composition inhabited by both the Serbs and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the interethnic relations like up until, let's say, the first multi-party elections? Let's pinpoint the time there.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, in Benkovac municipality, there were good interethnic relations. There might have been some minor disagreements but they were very proper relations. And people, regardless of their ethnic affiliation, they worked together, socialised, lived a normal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know -- can you give us the percentages of Croats and Serbs living in Benkovac municipality and the figures for the town of Benkovac itself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: As to the town of Benkovac itself, Benkovac was located in the centre of Benkovac municipality territory, and it was the Serb villages that gravitated towards that centre. So in the municipal headquarters of Benkovac or, rather, the centre of Benkovac, there were about -- Serbs accounted for 75 to 80 per cent. And a large number of officers were there too. We had a large barracks with a large number of officers who were mostly of different ethnic groups. Now, since the Serb ethnic group was the most numerous ethnic group in the former Yugoslavia, then this ratio was reflected among the officer cadres which means that they made up 75 or 80 per cent of the cadre compared to 20 or 25 per cent of others; whereas in the municipality, Serbs accounted for 48 per cent and Croat -- or Serbs for 52 per cent, I beg your pardon, and Croats 48 per cent of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To avoid any misunderstandings or lack of clarity, when you spoke about the percentage of the population in Benkovac and the different groups, did I understand you correctly to say that the Serbs, percentage of Serb population compared to the Croat population, included the number of Serb officers living in Benkovac? That went up to make that percentage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, because they lived there. The officers lived there with their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the relationship amongst the population was normal. When you say normal, normal relations, were these normal relations upset at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were upset. In a very short period of time, they became drastically upset, with the appearance of the nationalist parties or rather political parties with a nationalistic stream, through the information media, which were in the hands of the political parties of Croatia. These relations were also disturbed through the celebrations of the new year in 1990, when nobody expected to see the Croatian people, especially in purely Croatian villages, that they would, with the use of arms, instill fear. They would celebrate the new year festivities but they instilled fear among the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that at one point, relations with disturbed and upset and as an example of that you quoted the new year celebrations. Explain to us why relations were upset through the new year's celebrations? Why were the Serbs upset by these celebrations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The similar celebrations were up to that point of the kind that was quite normal throughout the world. At a certain point in time, through certain channels, a sizeable amount of arms appeared in the hands of members of the political party who were of Croat ethnicity, and I'm speaking of the municipality of Benkovac. They fired shots from these weapons, and they heralded the arrival of an era that would be marked by insecurity and fear in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your earlier answer that the Croatian political parties upset the interethnic relations through the information media. In what way was this done?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Discussions were held on the origins of the Serbs in the area. Serbs on their part were of course fearful of what was to become of them in light of what they had come -- gone through during World War II. Chauvinistic mottoes were uttered, emblems and signs were used which instilled a certain amount of fear in the people in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that chauvinist slogans and emblems and signs were being used. Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: These were symbols dating back to World War II which symbolised fascist and nationalist Croatian beliefs. These were slogans such as "Serbs should be hung from trees" and so on and so forth. And they all dated back to World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The chequer-board, at the time in 1990, was it the official emblem of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. Your Honour, I let this go on for a little bit. It's not in the 65 ter summary, all this about emblems and symbols and the chequer-board. So at this point I object to further evidence on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Remember, Mr. Milovancevic, we have time constraints so try to stay on what is on the 65 ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of the relations which were upset. What happened after the first multi-party elections? What was the situation like? And I am meaning in terms of interethnic relations.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The situation grew steadily worse. As commander of the Territorial Defence, I sent every day reports to the headquarters in Split. I was duty-bound to report on the political and security developments and the situation in the area. The tensions escalated, and the general political and security situation deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does the term "barricades" ring any bells? Did you hear of them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When did you hear of them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: This was in the autumn of 1990, or, rather, end of August 1990. Since the Croatian people in the area of Krajina and therefore in the area of Benkovac too --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Since the Serbian people in the area of Krajina had no weapons whatsoever, and the Croatian side was continually arming itself, the representatives of the Serb people approached the military personnel, which meant the JNA, the TO, but also the police force, for protection. Since at the time there was the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and the JNA, we did not have a legal basis upon which we would be able to protect the people. That was why the people started organising themselves. One such form of self-organisation with a view to preventing the attacks from the Croatian paramilitary forces on civilians was the erecting of these barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just stated in your answer that the people were unarmed. What do you mean "unarmed"? What happened with the weapons held by the Territorial Defence of Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: In June of 1991 [as interpreted], or I don't remember the exact date, two officers from the Slobodan Macura [phoen] barracks in Benkovac --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. You mentioned officers. Can you tell us who they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The JNA officers. There were two officers; one of them was Dusan Dragicevic and the Branislav Ristic. Dragicevic was a major and he was the logistics officer of the brigade, assistant for logistics of the brigades. Captain Ristic was the security officer. They came to my house and asked that I surrender the keys to the warehouse of the TO, which was situated within the Benkovac barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: They asked you to hand over the keys to the warehouse, the depot, in the barracks. What was contained there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Weapons and ammunition, which, under the wartime assignment, belonged to the TO Benkovac, and which was or were kept in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, but before it gets too far away, there is a reference to June of 1991, at least as it appears on the transcript in English, and I wonder it might have been June of 1990. I just wonder if that could be clarified, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to thank my learned friend for this intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned June 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, June 1991. It wasn't in 1990. It was in 1991. The weapons were under the JNA control. We were unable to use it or to gain access to it without the consent of the JNA. It must have been an error if it featured in a document differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned barricades, you said that this was sometime in the end of August 1990, the multi-party elections were held in mid-1990. Now, you speak of an event and you believe that it took place in the month of June 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me put this question to you: As the TO commander, as the acting TO commander, what were your relations like with the staff in Split? Did you send reports to them? Did you receive orders and instructions from them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: All the way up until the 30th of July, 1997 [as interpreted], I was in constant touch with the command in Split. They knew that the weapons were relocated, taken somewhere else, and this wasn't only the case in Benkovac. There was the -- it wasn't -- this was the Benkovac weapons that were taken away, and there were weapons taken away from other municipalities as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I'm sorry to do this to you again. Like Mr. Black, I see there is a date 30th of July, 1997. Is that a misinterpretation or a misquotation? He says: "Up until the 30th of July, 1997, I was in constant touch with the command in Split."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for directing our attention to this, and please do always direct our attention if something like this happens again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which date did you say it was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The 30th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This was the way I heard it. It wasn't 1997, it was 1991. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What you've just said about the weapons belonging to the TO in Benkovac, Obrovac and other municipalities, did I understand you correctly to say that the JNA took the weapons out of the TO depots in the barracks and placed them elsewhere outside of your control?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you stated that you reported to the staff in Split, which staff did you have in mind? You also said that you were regularly in touch with them and sent reports to them.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: This was the territorial staff in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the mention of the 1st of May, 1991, mean something to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. On the 1st and 2nd of May, and in the days that followed, an armed conflict broke out in the area of Kakma and the village of Polaca. This is a village in the south of the area of Benkovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who the parties to the conflict were and were there any consequences of it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The village of Polaca was one of the larger villages in the area. It was predominantly inhabited by Croats. They no longer honoured, let me put it this way, or did not consider as theirs the police force that was present in the Benkovac police station. And of course, the police administration of Zadar set up some sort of a police station in the village of Polaca. Members of that police station, along the road from Benkovac to Polaca and Biograd, and in the side roads there, controlled the passing traffic. In controlling traffic, their main aim was to possibly find weapons on Serb citizens pulled over along these roads, in order for this to be an immediate cause of a conflict. There were skirmishes and frictions between the members of the Zadar police station and members of the SUP of Benkovac because that's what it was, SUP Benkovac. There were attempts at finding a solution to the problem with peaceful means. However, it broke out into a conflict, an armed conflict, which lasted for two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to the conflict, you stated that the conflict broke out between the Zadar police force and Benkovac police force. Before the outbreak of the conflict, where were these forces situated? How did it come about, the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: You see, the village of Polaca is surrounded by several purely Serb villages, which are located quite near to it. In these villages, the police from the SUP Benkovac was present on a daily basis, because the villagers there asked them to protect them from the mistreatment of the Croatian police along the roads. It was these two police forces that came into conflict, and it so happened that on the 2nd of May, the member of these parapolice forces of Croatia was killed. His name was Branko Lisica [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly to say that when Franko Lisica got killed at Polaca it was the police officers of Serb and the police officers of Croat ethnicities who came into conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: You see, of course, the police force from Benkovac had mostly Serbs on them but there were also Croats on the force. Whereas in Polaca there were these police formations that were only recently formed. They were -- they referred to themselves as "redarstvenici."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, I know it is not absolutely time yet, but at Judge Nosworthy's request may we adjourn and come back a little later? But before we do so, there was a reference to the 2nd of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the time, Your Honour, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no. I just want to say when we come back, can we look at that date at page 59, line 16, talking about the 2nd of May? I just want to know of which year. We can do that when we come back. We will take a short adjournment and come back at half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, before the break, you mentioned some events in which Franko Lisica was killed. You mentioned the beginning of May but you didn't give us the year. When was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. What happened immediately after that conflict? How was that whole affair settled?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: From the Croatian side, there were the Croatian forces, the Serb side had its own forces, Benkovac police and the other police, they took control of the hills, elevation points. And in the course of those three or four days, up until the 5th or 6th of May, there was an exchange of sporadic gun-fire, and life came to a standstill in the area. There were absolutely no activities, nothing going on at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any activities linked to those events? Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As commander of the Territorial Defence, every day and not only every day but round the clock, 24 hours, I gathered information and sent them on to my superior commands. I received information from people who were directly included in the events in the area. And the chief of police in Benkovac, I told the chief of police in Benkovac, Bosko Drazic, that I was negotiating with the Croatian representatives to try and solve the conflict in a peaceful way on behalf of the Serbs. I was representing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was that offer accepted and what happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. My offer was accepted and after that, we came into contact -- we contacted the Croatian side, the citizens from Polaca, I don't know how the police in Benkovac went about this. But anyway, we decided upon an exact time when the representative of Polaca, and we as the representatives of the rest of the territory, and I myself as a representative, to negotiate a cease-fire, and to have life and work return to normal in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you in fact hold these talks, and if so, what happened and what agreement was reached?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did conduct the talks. It was on the 6th of May at 8.00 a.m. From the Croatian side a man turned up --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The 6th of May, what year was that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: 1991 we are talking about. The representative of the other side was an esteemed citizen by the name of Bobanovic from Polaca. I think his first name was Franjo but I'm not sure. And we met in Djuro Miljevic's house. Djuro Miljevic was a respected citizen of the village of Jagodnja Gornja. And on that day, he had some festivities, so this added to the occasion. But there wasn't much to celebrate. We negotiated, we talked, the man knew me, he recognised me because I happened to go to the village from time to time. We cooperated with them. We had very good cooperation with them before the war, and we endeavoured to continue along those lines. We agreed to have the forces withdraw, that the villagers could go back to working the fields and going about their daily business, to ensure that traffic along the roads was normal and the man left. We set a sort of deadline. We said, We will stop straight away, and you stop straight away, or in a hour's time, or whatever we had negotiated. Everything was normal to the benefit of both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And did they respect the agreement later on? Was it adhered to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, for a short period of time, for a few days, people did go back to working in the fields. However, during the night, there were once again provocations using artillery weapons and so on. Now, how long that went on, but let's say it went on for seven to 10 days. I don't think that's important. Anyway, it was the season of working in the fields, the crop season and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with respect to your local commander, the commander of the Territorial Defence of Benkovac is concerned, during that month of May 1991, was it the peacetime formation of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There was just me and my associates, and I worked until 2.00 and we would go home as we would in peacetime. And then I collected up information and sent it on to Split, reported back to Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you collected information or gathered information and sent that information to Split, can you tell us what you mean? We can deduce what you mean, but tell us specifically what was the type of information you gathered and what was it that you informed the Territorial Defence, Croatian Territorial Defence about in Split?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: It was of a security and military nature, information of that kind, referring to what was going on in the territory of Benkovac municipality. I had to establish the facts to see what the situation was, to assess that information and to forward that information to my superior command. That was my job and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, how long did this peacetime formation of the Territorial Defence of Benkovac exist? When was it a peacetime structure?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, it existed in that form until the 15th of July. Yes, I think it was the 15th of July. That would be correct. 1991, of course. When we were called by the Prime Minister, I think it was, Milan Babic, to attend a meeting in Knin. We, the Territorial Defence commanders, were invited and the chiefs of police in the SAO Krajina municipalities. At the meeting itself, which was behind closed doors, if I can put it that way, we were informed about the security situation on the territory of the SAO Krajina, that is to say the territory that came out in favour of a certain type of autonomy that had to be given shape to politically. The information we were given, and of course this was followed by an order later on, that only the municipal staffs from the peacetime formations according to the different branches and services in the staffs and headquarters should be mobilised and come under combat readiness and measures governing combat readiness, that they should be on the alert for further engagement. Now, since the situation deteriorated from one day to the next, especially from the 15th to this key date of the 30th of July, 1991, on a daily basis, and there were quite a number of us, we were numerically superior, we gathered information and of course maintained contact with the JNA commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Mr. Babic called you to attend this meeting, you as TO commander and the others, and put forward the security situation. Now, can you tell us in a word what was the reason to mobilise the staffs of the TO in the area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The escalation of inter-ethnic relations on the territory of SAO Krajina and in Croatia. They had come to a head. They were out of control. So with a view to protecting the Serb population, mobilisation and Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honours, for that interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was it that happened on the 30th or 31st of July? Was there reason to call for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of July in the early hours of the morning, the duty officer of the TO Defence Staff of Benkovac, I think it was around 5.00 in the morning in actual fact, informed me that the women who were tending to the cattle and sheep along the border belt towards Biograd and towards Sibenik in part had noticed stepped up movement and the members of certain armed formations approaching the Serb villages. In fact, these were of course the paramilitary police forces of the MUP of the Republic of Croatia from the direction of the village of Vuksic, moving towards the Serbian villages, where an attack was launched, and the number of men was the strength of a company. Some 100 MUP Croatian MUP members against these villages, whereas the villages and villagers were totally unarmed and going about their daily business in the village. From the south axis, from the Biograd direction, towards Miranje Donje and Ceranje, these villages, a terrorist group attacked them. I think there were four men who attacked along that axis and from the village of Priste Donje [phoen] towards the Ceranje Gornje village and Ceranje Donje village there was another terrorist group that was launching an attack. I came to see what this was all about. I went to see it all, and there were two or three of these terrorists or they were engaged in sabotage activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did a conflict break out, a clash, with those forces, the burgeoning forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what it was about. The MUP, Croatian MUP forces, the company-strong force, marching along a broad belt, and these Serb villages were scattered about the hills so it was normal that the people who were standing watch at the barricades, some of them had hunting rifles, hunting weapons, they stopped at these by way of a warning. They wanted to issue a warning. And that was enough to these "redarstvenici" to in fact stop, whereas the members of the police who were the sole people to carry weapons, they had infantry weapons that they were issued, they wanted to help the people because there was general panic and fear among the people. So they distributed themselves around the area to help the people. I toured those areas. I was able to do so. So I spent some time touring the areas, and the police, the Milicija, went to help the people along this southern axis, but the group moving from the other direction attacked a village guard, a village watch that was standing up at the barricades there, and the people manning this village guard or village watch started to shoot and they killed one of the members of that group. We didn't know about this. We just learnt that he had been liquidated or killed five days later. Now, the group that was doing the attacking from the direction of Pristeg [phoen] towards the Gornji and Donji villages with several sabotage men in the middle of a field moved -- was moving forward and had already entered the region of the Serb villages, when the villagers who were on guard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was able to follow the movement of these three men engaged in sabotage activities. I had some binoculars and was able to see them using the binoculars. They were placed in an encirclement. They were set siege to by the villagers without any command. They had makeshift weapons, some sort of barrels or whatever, hunting rifles, and they surrounded this group of men engaged in this sabotage activity, and the group took refuge in an orchard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the group in fact stopped?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the group was stopped, during the night. So this went on the whole day and the group was finally blocked during the night, and in the morning hours when the members of the group wanted to break through the siege, the encirclement, they were fired at and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during that time, and you said that it happened on the 30th of July, 1991. So during that period in Benkovac, there was a JNA barracks, was there not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How many units were housed in those barracks?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: It's a large barracks which was able to accommodate these two large units, the size of a brigade, which means 5 or 6.000 men strong. There were two, two and a half, 3.000 soldiers there all the time, permanently. In peacetime, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what was situation like communication-wise, the roads that the JNA units used during that summer, the Benkovac area? Not only the barracks but also members of the JNA elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The command, the JNA command, demanded that all structures, civilians, non-commissioned officers, officers and so on, should do everything to keep the peace, to ensure that peace reigned and that the roads were passable, that you could move along the roads. However, the barricades were set up in the directions towards Zadar and Sibenik and the villages but -- and these barricades would be erected during the nights, because the villagers were afraid, and then they would be dismantled in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that during the night barricades would appear, would be erected in the villages and that they would be dismantled in the morning, in what villages did this take place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, barricades would be erected between three or four Serb villages. There wasn't any -- it was mostly out of fear. Those villages were of the same ethnic composition. We gave orders to some companies, such as the roadworks company and so on, to dismantle them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we are talking about the summer of 1991, in addition to those barricades, were there any other provocations or firing or disruption of traffic along the roads in any way, anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: As commander of the Territorial Defence, I did not directly take part in any JNA activities. I wasn't able to do so. The JNA had problems to de-block their barracks in Zadar and Sibenik. That was going on in the autumn of 1991. And after the agreement reached between the government of the Republic of Croatia and the SFRY Presidency, to the effect that the JNA would be able to pull out its men and materiel from barracks in Croatia, the Zemunik airport and the barracks were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the agreement reached between the SFRY Presidency and the government of Croatia to de-block the barricades. When did that happen? You said the autumn of 1991 but could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The autumn of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the agreement honoured?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't. The agreement wasn't honoured in the area of Benkovac municipality. This is a well-known story. The action which involved pulling out the equipment was obstructed by the Croatian side, and they went even as far as destroying the materiel just to prevent it from leaving the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which Croatian forces obstructed the pulling out of the military materiel and where was this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: These were the paramilitary forces of the ZNG, the police forces, the reserve police force of the Republic of Croatia. The villages involved were Skabrnja and Nadin -- or, rather, the Nadinska Gradina installations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In what way was the pulling out of the JNA equipment obstructed from these villages?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The obstruction consisted of artillery weapons and anti-aircraft weapons. Very often they would also obstruct the sorties of cargo aircraft from Udbina because they were shot at from anti-aircraft weapons of 12.7 calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned anti-aircraft guns and anti-aircraft machine-guns. Where were these weapons positioned and where was the fire opened from?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The main feature was Nadinska Gradina. This was an elevated feature which was a fortified building dating back to I don't know which century and it was practically invincible. It was from this vantage point that they opened fire on the Benkovac-Zadar road which passes through the area. From this hill, they also fired upon cargo aircraft which took off from the airport this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where you got this information from, and I mean the information concerning the weapons and forces involved in the shooting and concerning the consequences of the fire.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, we had several sources. First of all, we observed the area and then there were the JNA forces there which tried to neutralise the weapons. We also had vehicles which were damaged and shot at from weapons of a certain calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You stated that JNA convoys were being attacked. Is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Of course. We only used the roads to pull out the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which sort of hardware and where was it from that the JNA tried to pull out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, we had the air force academy, the school system, the airfield there. There were fuel depots for helicopters and aircraft there that we had. So these were enormous quantities of materiel. In order to avoid these obstructions and provocations, the army built a new road through some fields. However, the Croatian forces opened fire on that road as well. Some 15 to 20 drivers and members of the escort were killed just during the period when the materiel was being pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The road across the fields built by the army, where was it start -- where was its starting point and which route did it take?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: From the Zemunik airport, therefore the northern side of the Zemunik airport, through Smokovici village, Vocnjak, all the way up to Gornji Zemunik, and then on to the village of Smilcic, across Debela Brdo, toward Knin and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify once again why the road was built across the field?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, because we couldn't use the regular roads as we should have been able to pursuant to the agreement between the Croatian government and the SFRY Presidency. However, we were unable to because people got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the fact that some 15 to 20 people got killed along that new road. On which side was this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: On our side. These were truck drivers, members of the army who escorted the convoys. These would be people who provided security to the convoy, and when the Croatian forces opened fire, they were the casualties of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Nadinska Kosa and Skabrnja. Were these villages to be found in the Benkovac municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Nadin, yes. Nadin was a mixed village, as far as its ethnic makeup goes, but most of the inhabitants were Croats. Serbs had left the area earlier on because of the presence of the Croatian paramilitary forces. Only Croats stayed behind in Nadin. Skabrnja is a village in the municipality of Zadar, and it is economically speaking the wealthiest village, the most affluent village, and it lay on the border of the Zadar municipality and Benkovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You stated that Skabrnja was the strongest Croatian village. Where did that village get anti-aircraft machine-guns, anti-aircraft guns and other weaponry they handled?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know where they got the weapons from. But based on reconnaissance we were able to see that they had the weapons, and later on we also seized these weapons. You asked me where we got the information from. Well, I was in the position to listen in to a conversation between the Chief of the General Staff, General Kadijevic, and General Ratko Mladic. He was their general already. He happened to be in the command of the 180th Brigade, and at that meeting, where I was invited also as a commander of the TO, we were informed of the security situation. At that point, General Mladic was called to speak over the phone to the General Staff, with General Adzic, and most of the officers were required to leave the conference room because they weren't allowed to listen to the conversation. I stayed behind, as did all the commanders, and General Adzic asked why it was that JNA aircraft landed in Belgrade damaged. They obviously came under fire and became damaged. General Mladic told him that he didn't have any information about it, but that he was to inquire after that, after this, and that he would report back to them in the General Staff in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes the name wasn't Kadijevic but Adzic earlier.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: In this conversation which lasted some 15 minutes, General Adzic asked of General Mladic to do his best to try to establish contacts with the Croatian side peacefully and to inform them of the existence of the agreement concerning the pulling out of the equipment. Now what I'm telling you about took place some 10 days before the armed conflict in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know anything about the action conducted in the village of Skabrnja in the month of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: I do. Everything that had to do with the Territorial Defence and all the subsequent events in Skabrnja are well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you came to know this, and whether the Territorial Defence had to do anything with the action in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Territorial Defence had indirectly to do with the action, but let me first explain how the preparations concerning the action took place. In the evening hours, at about 6.00 or 7.00 in the evening, in the month of November --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the date.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: I was invited there as the commander of the TO and Drazic as chief of police in Benkovac too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreter didn't hear the date in November. In the evening hours at about 6.00 or 7.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of which year? 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Yes, yes, in 1991, that was the 17th of November. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can I please ask you to always mention the year when indicating a date.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you received an invitation. Where it was that you went and what did you find out there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: I was invited by the Chief of Staff of 180th Brigade, Lieutenant-Colonel Momcilo Vojinovic -- Bogunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that this was in the evening hours on the 17th of November, 1991. What did Lieutenant-Colonel Bogunovic tell you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Bogunovic told us that an activity was being prepared and that he had a task for us as the TO, in view of our abilities and establishment. The operations officer at the time, Lieutenant-Colonel Babic, I can't remember his first name, tabled a plan and said that the TO commanders had the task of raising the combat readiness of TO units opposite the separation line between Croatian and Serb forces on the Skabrnja axis. To me, it meant that the village guards should refrain from standing guard at the time when a JNA operation was in course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mention the village guards, that they should have been activated. Where were they? In which villages?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: These were the villages of the western part of the Benkovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sorry, did the witness say they should have been activated?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know if I quoted the witness properly. Let me rephrase it. I apologise if I was not precise enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You were given the task -- when mentioning a unit or a village, please tell us what this is specifically about. Which village guard, units, did you have in mind as the TO commander?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The TO squad of the local commune of Biljana Donja. This was a squad of some ten people. The squad in the village of Veljane or Veljanska Kosa [phoen], the squad at Milcici [phoen]. These were the villages bordering the Zadar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I interrupted you. Please tell us and describe for us what your task was and what you were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: We were informed of the fact that the Yugoslav People's Army would -- was tasked to group its forces and not to have a show of force in terms of opening fire, but simply by its presence in the area of the village of Skabrnja that it should come into contact with the representatives of the Croatian armed forces, the ZNG, or whichever other force was there, and to hold talks with them. Specific officers were designated who were given a list of issues upon which the discussion was to take place. The objective was to warn the Croatian forces that they ought no longer to open fire on the convoys and the aircraft that had previously been opened fire on, that the Croatian forces should retreat from the area and, pursuant to the agreement that was signed, the political agreement, that they allow the road to be passable. The task was, as concerns the JNA infantry, all active duty officers of the JNA took part in the operation, and the unit was some 80 men strong. And as far as the used assets were concerned, there was artillery and a mechanised unit with some eight to nine APCs. The tank crews consisted solely of active-duty recruits, conscripts, who were doing their obligatory military service. Officers were also active-duty JNA personnel. Some of the APC crews were manned to the full strength from TO ranks but not the TO Benkovac but rather from Bosnia, from Smederevo in Serbia and so on and so forth, and these were people holding specific specialties as -- for these APCs. These soldiers, members of the reserve force, who ended up in the Benkovac area, were put up at the Smilcic economy farm. They had been brought over there several days earlier. I was there on the spot some four to five days before because I wanted to show the commander for moral guidance of the 9th Corps the way over there. It was already night-time, and I took him over to those men who were supposedly there as reinforcements, and they wanted to go back home because they had been mobilised for quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. You said that these were soldiers mobilised into the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, only the JNA and they were not just from Croatia. They came from all over, even from Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned taking this officer to see them. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: That was Colonel Mesud -- I can't remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it Mesud Hasotic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mesud Hasotic. I was there when he talked to them, and he told them this: Lads, in a few days time, and I didn't know which day, in fact, you are going to carry out a very simple task which isn't going to involve any combat, and after that you're going to go home. There is nothing for you to complain about because nobody is going to get hurt, nothing will happen to you. And he managed to calm them down. And now let me go back to Skabrnja to the composition of the forces there, including the reserve force. The commander of the forces, including tanks and APCs was Miodrag Stevanovic. He was a lieutenant, an active-duty officer. He had under him young lads who were conscripts, who were doing their military service. His task was to use a megaphone while mounted on a tank and to call upon those present in Skabrnja and to ask them to turn around their barrels and not to open fire. One of the soldiers was also holding a flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of the officer --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You're mentioning the JNA officer Stevanovic and the JNA soldier?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, member of the JNA. They are all members of the JNA. So was the officer. As the column went past the western part of Skabrnja --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, pause there. Can you please first wait for Miodrag to put the question to you. So on the 17th of November, 1991, you were summoned to the staff with Lieutenant-Colonel Bogunovic, and this is what was told to you. You were told this on the 17th of November?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When was the action scheduled to begin?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: On the following morning, on the 18th, at 8.00, right after the orders were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened on the following day, on the 18th of November? When did the action commence and how? Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The unit set off from this farm at Smilcici where the reserve force were and went along the following route, Smilcic, Zemunik Gornji with a view to turning over to Skabrnja. Things went and took their normal course. I was in Smiljani Donji, and together with all the other officers who were assigned to be there, I followed the entire operation over the communications means -- devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the unit set off from Smilcici. Was it a JNA unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before we move on to describing the events, tell us, please, how many forces the Territorial Defence had, how many were they included in that operation and where were those forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: In addition to the forces of the local communes or those villages, those 15 or 20 men whose task it was to secure -- provide security for the various clinics and transformer stations and so on, it was my task, it was my duty, and I was given this as an assignment in fact, to prepare for an escalation. Should there be an escalation, to be prepared. But everything should be done to prevent the worst from happening and to protect my Territorial Defence units in those villages and the civilians in the territory of Benkovac municipality. In the morning, I ordered a squad of -- numbering some 12 men, an anti-sabotage unit, one that existed in peacetime as well, to use a minibus, a van, and relocate to Biljani Donji, and that unit was escorted by two mortars, 82-millimetre mortars with crews, and this was following regulations as is usually done. And as an escort with the medical corps, to have an ambulance as well under the command of the commander n-- or, rather, Nada Pupovac was in charge of the ambulance, and she was in charge of the medical corps duties in peacetime. They came to where I was, that is to say the Biljani Donji region, where the JNA officers were, who were on some assignment there, and I was able to follow the whole situation through our communications system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have described the forces to us. How many men were there in the Territorial Defence that you had assigned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, 25 to 30 men roughly. They were engaged either directly or in preparation, in waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that those forces were in the same locality that you were in. So could you tell us again where were those forces deployed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: They were deployed at Biljani Donji, the Skoric hamlet, right next to the road, next to the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How far is that from the village of Skabrnja itself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: As the crow flies, two kilometres, two or three kilometres, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And when did that TO unit of yours, if I can call it that, those 25 or 30 men, when did they arrive at Biljani Donji, on what day, when?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: In the morning, before 7.00 a.m., on the 18th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that in the morning, the JNA unit had set out. Could you tell us once again what that JNA unit was composed of, the one advancing towards Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: I've already said it was composed of mechanised infantry, eight or nine transporters in all, APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what a mechanised infantry means?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: They are infantry men, soldiers, which are transported to the battlefield, and they use the resources of an APC as technical equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So there were seven or eight of these APCs. How many tanks were there? You mentioned tanks.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: There were three tanks, and they were provided just to have a show of force, to show that the JNA was powerful and could use them if the need arose. They had their crews.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now you said that they set out from their base at 7.00 in the morning. How do you know that, and how do you know what route they took?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: I know that because I was on the spot when they set out. I was on the spot in -- at that facility, at that factory farm, and all the JNA officers who were at Biljana Donji later on took a different route and reached Biljani Donji in the space of five minutes. So I was there when they set out, I took another route, and I was there when they arrived. I didn't escort them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what happened to this JNA column with the three tanks and seven or eight APCs that you described when they arrived in Skabrnja? Which route did they take, where did they, what places did they pass through, and what happened in Skabrnja, if you can tell us that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That column reached the junction of Zemunik Gornji, Skabrnja Zadar. And they set off, they took the left road through the hamlet called Ambar [phoen] and they were all Croats there. We received information that they waved to the army as they passed. So they were moving ahead with good intentions. Now, this hamlet called Ambar is a hamlet that is 300 or 400 -- stretches for a distance of 300 or 400 metres. Then you get to the road, the main road, and you come to the entrance, the central portion, rather, of Skabrnja - I call at a time central portion - linking Biljani Donji to Zadar. So it's that 300 or 400 or 500 metres at most. It's that stretch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now up until that point, did anybody open fire at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: No. Everything was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: When the column reached the junction of Biljani Donji and Zadar, the crossroads, because you can get to Skabrnja taking both those directions, that was the crossroads, and the column was stopped there, and according to the information I had, a Lieutenant Stevanovic got off the APC he was in, took up a megaphone, and the soldier next to him got down carrying a flag, because they saw some people some 50 or 60 metres in front of them. Their intention was to warn them, they turned off the engines and they wanted to contact the people to warn them. At that point in time, somebody on the Croatian side hit the lieutenant in the head or face. His name Stevanovic. Now, as that happened, immediately in front of the first car, the soldier carrying the flag, he was a Muslim, went up to help him but they killed him too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who did they kill? Or, rather, who killed him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The paramilitary forces of Skabrnja, the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Chaos erupted, and it lasted for about half an hour. There was general chaos for a short time, maybe not even half an hour, during which time both sides opened fire. There was shooting from both sides. The JNA officers from Biljani Donji gave express orders for a cease-fire straight away. They couldn't stop shooting because the Croatian side started shooting more and more fiercely. At one point the Croatian forces did stop firing and there was a general lull.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the firing went on for about half an hour. So after that half hour of shooting from both sides, there was a lull; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: This is how it was. The command of the brigade in Benkovac where Lieutenant-Colonel Bogunovic was in command was informed, and they asked the command of the 9th Corps to issue further orders, according to which this unit should either return, asking whether the unit was to return, or to maintain that position and -- or to advance. Those were the three possibilities open to them. Now, Major Djurica Janko, an active-duty officer, the commander of the artillery in Benkovac, platoon in Benkovac, had probably received orders from the command in Benkovac to go down there and resolve the situation, to have peace and quiet return. Major Djurica sets off, and there is no shooting. The talks last for 10 to 15 minutes. They await further orders. Now, at that moment, probably the Croatian forces had consolidated, and launched an organised attack on that column of vehicles, the APCs and the rest. At that moment, everybody had taken up their positions in the tanks and the APCs, and there was an all-out conflict in which both sides opened fire. Now, as the situation escalated, contacts were being made with the Croatian side to cease hostilities, and according to our information the Croatian side did not want to halt hostilities and to cease fire. Because of all the people who had been killed and wounded and the attacks launched on the equipment and materiel, the unit continued to advance towards Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How long did that combat activity go on for on that 18th of November, 1991? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: They went on the whole day until dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you something now, Mr. Lakic, and it is this: You were in another locality. You were -- how do you know about all this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: I entered Skabrnja when the action ceased. Now, from my men, my reserve men, became forces to enable the civilian population of Skabrnja to pull out, and the ambulance pulled out, the wounded soldiers, but also the civilians. The minibus or van that brought my squad in, the anti-sabotage unit, pulled out women, children, the elderly from Skabrnja on five or six occasions, five or six times. And when the conflict subsided or rather ended at around 5.00 p.m., the Croatian forces had withdrawn, and I entered Skabrnja because I thought there were still some more civilians left, and I wanted to try to evacuate those civilians during the night. The people that we found actually had already been evacuated and put up into the primary school building, the children's nursery school, and various other facilities belonging to the civilian protection organisation. They numbered about 120 or 30 civilians, women, children and elderly. Of course, and I was personally there, I asked them what shall we do with you? What's your proposal? What do you want us to do with you? Their proposal was that they could cross over to the Croatian side to join their people. I asked the transport company of Benkovac to give us -- provide us with buses and they were transported to the nearest border point leading to the Croatian forces. And during the night, 7.00, 8.00, 9.00 p.m., these civilians were taken to this border belt so that they could cross over on to the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that about 100 civilians, the inhabitants of Skabrnja, were evacuated by the members of the Territorial Defence --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: -- during the fighting itself. Can you tell us how many inhabitants the village of Skabrnja actually had at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact figure but I think over 2.000. At least over 2.000 inhabitants. It's a large village covering quite a large territory, so certainly some 2.000 inhabitants. But -- well, yes, I'll stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You managed to evacuate more than 100 people. What happened to the other civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: This is what happened. The other civilians, probably members of the armed forces of those paramilitaries of Croatia as well withdrew towards the railway station in Skabrnja, towards the fields and the village of Prkos. They withdrew, they were withdrawing, leaving the village. Nobody fired at them. We received information that they were withdrawing but there was no artillery fire at them. So there were no casualties. They were allowed to withdraw safely and securely and leave the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When, in -- during that afternoon, or early evening, on the 18th of November, 1991, you arrived in Skabrnja, did you happen to see whether there were any casualties?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: I saw two or three casualties. They were conscripts, soldiers, they had their military belts on them. They had some -- they were wearing camouflage uniforms, and they were lying by the main road leading into Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These people in these uniforms and military belts, who did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The armed formations of the unit in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that this movement of JNA units towards Skabrnja began at 7.00 in the morning. Before the JNA unit entered Skabrnja, was artillery fire opened targeting Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: No, not a single bullet was fired, absolutely not. Because the aim was different. It was -- the aim was to resolve the problem peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, about these artillery units, do you know how many of those artillery units there were and how many men made them up?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, not much, because the JNA hadn't been planning on engaging them. I know that there were some howitzer units, one or two howitzers actually, and a mortar platoon, 120-millimetre mortar platoon. It existed formation-wise but otherwise I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, give us some figures or at least an assessment, of the total number of forces, how many men in total, JNA soldiers, took part, including the artillery?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, 80 -- about 80 in the column, let's say approximately 80, perhaps 20 or 30 more in those -- with those two or three vehicles and equipment. I really can't say more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the strength of the Croatian forces in Skabrnja at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: I think that they didn't have many men at the time. There were mostly those who had been on duty during the night and that morning. But the forces in Skabrnja, up to Nadinska Gradina had five companies; their strength was five companies. Now, the unit which provided security for those three villages in that line, in that chain, was the 5th Company, known as the Skabrnja Battalion, and it had the most sophisticated infantry weapons, we later established that, and everything else, all the accompanying artillery, armoured facilities. It was an armoured unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that it was equipped in that way, what did that mean specifically? Can you describe to us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, automatic rifles, pistols, snipers, right up to a 12.7-calibre weapon. Above that calibre, you have artillery weapons. So, which would mean 82-millimetre mortars, 120 is artillery, anti-aircraft guns. We found the Maljutka type of weapon and things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say we found Maljutkas, where did you find these Maljutkas and what are Maljutkas?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't find them because I didn't search for them. What I meant was that the JNA forces came across them, and they brought them to the garrison in Benkovac and laid them out there, exhibited them, and I saw them with my own eyes. So that's what we found when we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What are Maljutkas?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Anti-armour rockets of Russian origin but they were produced by the JNA, or rather, in Yugoslavia, by Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, what's the spelling because it seems to be absent from the transcript and the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maljutka, m-a-l-j-u-t-k-a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You stated that your task, as Territorial Defence, was to stay on the side --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please wait for my question, otherwise the interpreters won't be able to catch up. You said that you were in Biljani Donji with your men from the TO, some 25 to 30 of them. When did your men join the operation in Skabrnja? You stated that your men were pulling out civilians.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, as soon as there were first casualties, first wounded people, my men came up to me and said, We have civilians wounded. What are we going to do with them? The JNA wasn't prepared for such a situation. I had that Volkswagen van and two to three people from the medical corps, and a minibus, which belonged to a commercial company from Benkovac, which had some 20 seats, and I ordered straight away that the population be given medical assistance and evacuated in order to get them out of harm's way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you about the composition of the units participating in the action. Did they include members of the SAO Krajina Police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The police was given a task which was of its regular nature, and that was to conduct traffic control in the area, as per normal, and together with the TO to maintain law and order in these villages, and in the eventuality that a sole, free agent, should appear, or anyone disrupting law and order, to apply measures that were normally applied in such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was the police assigned its tasks and by whom, and which specific police force was involved?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the police of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I meant the locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was your question answered, Mr. Milovancevic? You asked: "I asked you about the composition of the units participating in the action. Did they include members of the SAO Krajina Police?" I'm not quite sure that what came after that answers that question. If it does [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted, in fact, to pursue the matter further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not directly involved, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The task that you were given on the 17th of November, 1991, from Lieutenant-Colonel Bogunovic, in the evening hours, when was this task passed on to the police force and to which specific units in which town?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The task was given to the professional police force in the public security station in Benkovac, chief of police Bosko was given that particular assignment on the same day I was. On the 17th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many police officers were assigned to that particular mission and did they join the JNA police on its -- the JNA unit on its way to Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: No, they did not go alongside the JNA units, nor would they be allowed to. There was no need for that. The police unit did not go to Skabrnja at all. They had no business there. Their business was to do their regular policing duties in the area of Benkovac, where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The size of the police force in Benkovac who had to carry out these duties in these villages, do you know what it was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: In my assessment, some 15 to 20 of them. These were traffic patrols and regular police patrols, seeing to it that law and order were maintained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You stated that at the end of the day, on the 18th of November, 1991, when the hostilities ceased, you arrived in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when the operation in Skabrnja ended?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: The action formally ended on the 19th, but in actual fact it ended on the 18th. On the 19th, I was no longer in the area and there were no longer any combat activities anymore. If there were, they were sporadic and they did not result in any casualties. Therefore, the action took place over the two days -- or, rather, the task wasn't accomplished at all, but the action was halted at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the losses suffered on the JNA side and whether the TO suffered any losses and what the losses were on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC
utterances.text: I think that on the JNA side, there were two persons killed, the lieutenant -- or second lieutenant and his soldier, and there were several slightly wounded, two or three or five at most. There were no casualties among the TO ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise for the microphone. But it seems to me that we have come to the end of the day. Perhaps this would be a convenient time to stop for the day and continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't want to ask that last question that you had, for which you didn't have a microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will have to deal with this topic tomorrow as well, so there is no need to broach it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Very well then. That brings us to the end of the day today. The matter is going to stand adjourned to tomorrow at 9.00 in the same court. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
